Mechanical record · slides 3–19

Fixed prosthodontics and the principles of tooth preparation

  • Fixed prosthodontics MR 3: restorations that are cemented into place and are not readily removable. They range from a single tooth to an entire arch.
  • Purposes MR 6: restore masticatory function, improve appearance, improve speech, promote good oral hygiene, and stabilize the arch and occlusion.

Contraindications MR 8

Lack of supporting alveolar bone · periodontal disease · excessive mobility of abutment teeth · no interest in oral hygiene · patient can’t afford it.

Materials MR 10

Metallic: gold alloy, base metal alloy, porcelain fused to metal (PFM). Non-metallic: porcelain, composite resin, hybrid.

Types MR 9: porcelain veneers, direct and indirect resin veneers, bridges, inlays, onlays, partial crowns and full-cast crowns.

The three principles MR 15

PrincipleWhat it governs
BiologicHealth of the oral tissues
MechanicalIntegrity and durability of the restoration
EstheticAppearance of the patient

Principles of tooth reduction MR 17 BE 15

Path of insertion · retention and resistance · structural durability · reduce sound tooth structure as little as possible · remove decay · outline form.

Mechanical considerations MR 19

Retention · resistance features · path of insertion · structural durability.

BLAT: Bone, Loose, Apathy, Tight budgetThe contraindications: no supporting bone or periodontal disease, mobile abutments, no hygiene interest, can’t afford it.
B-M-E = Body, Machine, EyeBiologic protects the body’s tissues, mechanical keeps the machine working, esthetic pleases the eye.
PFM sits in the metallic column on MR 10; hybrid sits with porcelain and composite resin in the non-metallic column. The mechanical principle governs the restoration’s integrity; the biologic principle governs the tissues.

Mechanical record · slides 20–31

Path of insertion

  • Path of insertion MR 20: the direction through which the restoration can be precisely seated on the prepared tooth or teeth. Without one, the wax pattern distorts or the restoration fails to seat.
  • Line of insertion MR 22: a single direction of seating. It needs parallel opposing axial surfaces, so any deviation stops the restoration seating.
  • Range of insertion MR 25: the converging angle of two opposing surfaces; the restoration seats in any direction within it.

Bridges: a common path MR 26–31

Common line of insertion MR 26

One direction through which all retainers of a fixed-fixed bridge can be seated.

Common range of insertion MR 31

The sum of the smallest converging angles of the mesial plus distal abutment surfaces, within which all retainers seat.

Checking the path MR 27–30: sight the preparation with one eye along the intended path, directly or in a mirror; check bridge abutments together on the cast. In the occlusal view, any wall hidden under the occlusal outline is an undercut.

Line = one door, range = a doorwayA line allows exactly one direction; a range allows any direction inside the convergence angle.
The common range is the sum of the smallest converging angles, mesial plus distal, not the largest and not an average.

Mechanical record · slides 32–52

Factors that set the path of insertion

Five factors MR 32: reduction of the axial surfaces · rounding of the axial line angles · proximal grooves · ledges and indentations · pinholes.

Axial reduction MR 33–34

  • Buccal and lingual surfaces: remove the infrabulge, the undercut below the height of contour.
  • Mesial and distal surfaces: they naturally diverge occlusally; remove that divergence.
  • Line angles MR 35–36: preparing each surface separately leaves four cervical triangular undercuts. Rounding the line angles removes them, sets the path, and carries a continuous finish line into the gingival crevice.

Axial grooves MR 37–45

Where MR 37

¾ crown: mesial and distal grooves. ½ crown: buccal and lingual grooves.

Walls MR 38

Buccal, lingual, axial, and a gingival seat.

  1. Buccal and lingual walls parallel to each other or slightly divergent occlusally MR 44.
  2. Lingual wall parallel or slightly convergent with the lingual surface.
  3. Buccal wall may converge or diverge freely.
  4. Axial wall parallel to the opposing proximal surface, or slightly convergent MR 45.

Mandibular and maxillary ¾ crowns are shown on MR 40; the lower ¾ crown has an extension on the buccal surface MR 41; the seven-eighths crown is on MR 42, and the MOD onlay on MR 39.

Pin-ledge MR 47–52

  • An anterior partial-coverage retainer. The palatal surface carries two ledges and three indentations MR 47.
  • In a splinting bridge, a proximal groove or slice takes the connector MR 48.
  • Pinhole dimensions MR 50: about 2 mm deep, with 0.5 mm and 1 mm clearances shown on the drawing; a slice carries the connector.
  • Pinholes MR 49: two incisal and one gingival. They are parallel to each other, to the incisal 2/3 of the tooth (the path), to the mid-sagittal plane and to the fronto-axial plane.
¾ = M & D, ½ = B & LThree-quarter crowns take mesial and distal grooves; half crowns take buccal and lingual grooves.
Pin-ledge: pins 2–1, ledges 2–3Two incisal pinholes and one gingival; two ledges and three indentations.
Mesial and distal surfaces diverge occlusally; buccal and lingual surfaces have an infrabulge undercut. Only the buccal groove wall is free to converge or diverge.

Mechanical record 54–76 · Biological record 5–14

Retention and resistance

Forces on a prosthesis MR 56–58

Tipping · twisting (rotational) · forces along the path of insertion: apical when closing on a bolus, occlusal when the mandible opens with sticky food between the prosthesis and the opposing teeth.

Definitions MR 59

Retention prevents removal along the path of insertion. Resistance prevents dislodgement by apical, oblique or horizontal forces.

We study occlusal forces so the preparation has adequate retention and resistance form and structural durability MR 55. Retention form depends on the magnitude of dislodging forces and the geometry of the preparation, starting with taper MR 62.

Tipping path MR 60: the arc along which the crown would rotate off the tooth. Tooth structure that lies outside the arc resists it. The fulcrum is the finish line on the opposite side MR 67.

Retentive features MR 63: friction between opposing axial walls · axial grooves · pinholes · ledges and indentations · a post hole in the root canal.

What raises or lowers resistance MR 65–76

FactorRule from the lecture
Axial height MR 67Occlusal reduction ≤ one-third of the occlusogingival height
Short teeth MR 68Extend the finish line subgingivally; prepare with less taper
Taper MR 69Ideal total convergence 3–5°; excess taper resists less
Diameter MR 72Same height and taper: the smaller-diameter tooth resists tipping better
Surface area MR 73Counts most when it adds axial wall length
Circumferential irregularity MR 74Natural irregularity resists tipping and twisting; add boxes or grooves to round, short or over-tapered teeth
Occlusal irregularity MR 75Anatomic reduction helps; flat reduction wastes height; pinholes can be added
Adaptation MR 76A small space helps seating; excessive space leaves it to the cement and lowers resistance

Grooves and boxes BE 7–12

  • V-shaped groove: tends to be displaced by horizontal force. U-shaped: its lingual wall sits on the proximal surface and a thick rib of metal resists. Box: used with proximal caries and beside a solder joint BE 7.
  • The groove’s relation to the tipping path depends on its length, position and depth BE 8. A longer groove retains more; a groove placed more buccally leaves more tooth lingual to it BE 10; a deeper U or box form resists better than a V BE 11.
  • Boxes are more effective but need bulk; grooves suit anteriors and mandibular premolars; a box goes at the mid-proximal of full-veneer abutments BE 11–12.
  • Pin-ledge: biting on the pontic gives incisogingival and linguolabial stresses; lingual ledges resist tissue-ward movement BE 13–14.
Retention = Removal along the RoadRetention stops the crown coming off along its own path; resistance stops everything else.
3 to 5 stays aliveThe mechanical lecture’s ideal total convergence is 3–5°.
V Vanishes, U Unbudges, Box BestV grooves get displaced; U grooves resist with a metal rib; boxes are most effective.
Two taper numbers: 3–5° is the mechanical lecture’s ideal (MR 69); 5–15° is the all-ceramic guideline slide (CP 136). A smaller diameter resists tipping better.

Biological record · slides 17–23

Structural durability

The restoration must be thick enough to resist deformation. Deformation is prevented by alloy selection and adequate tooth reduction BE 20.

Occlusal reduction BE 18

At least 1–1.5 mm for rigidity. The functional cusp bevel is an integral part of it; without it the casting is thin or perforated.

Axial reduction BE 19

0.3–0.5 mm at the cervical, increasing to 1 mm towards occlusal for a metal casting; more when ceramic veneers the metal.

Preparation features and the principle each serves BE 23

FeaturePrinciple
Axial reductionRetention and resistance, structural durability
Concave cingulum reductionStructural durability
Vertical lingual wallRetention and resistance
Rounded line anglesStructural durability
Modified shoulderMarginal integrity, durability, periodontal preservation, resistance
1–1.5 on top, 0.3 to 1 on the sidesCasting: occlusal 1–1.5 mm; axial 0.3–0.5 mm at the cervical rising to 1 mm.
The functional cusp bevel is part of occlusal reduction, not an optional extra. Axial reduction for metal is less than for metal-ceramic.

Biological record · slides 25–34, 43–44

Biologic considerations: protect the pulp, teeth and tissues

Easily damaged BE 28

The adjacent teeth, the soft tissues and the pulp.

Pulp injury BE 27

Temperature from friction of rotary instruments · chemical action of bases, restorative resin, luting agents and solvents · bacterial action from microleakage.

The adjacent tooth BE 30–34: a needle stone placed wrongly in the contact area injures the neighbour. Keep it inside the tooth being prepared, leaving a thin sliver of its own enamel to protect the neighbour.

Heat, Chemicals, BugsThe three ways preparation injures the pulp: temperature, chemical action, bacterial microleakage.
Needle Nicks NeighboursA badly placed needle stone scars the adjacent tooth.
Luting agents and solvents are chemical injuries; microleakage is bacterial; friction is temperature.

Biological record · slides 35–51

Conservation of tooth structure and future dental health

Guidelines for conservation BE 37–38

  1. Partial coverage rather than complete coverage where possible.
  2. The minimum convergence angle between axial walls.
  3. Uniform occlusal and axial reduction, with withdrawal along the long axis.
  4. A conservative margin.
  5. No unnecessary extension.

How a poor preparation harms long-term health BE 39

  • Insufficient axial reduction → an over-contoured restoration → plaque → periodontal disease or caries.
  • Inadequate occlusal reduction → occlusal dysfunction.
  • Poor margin placement → chipped enamel or cusp fracture.

Preventing fracture BE 40

An onlay protects better than an inlay; a complete crown protects best by holding the cusps together.

Extension for protection BE 41

Remove undermined enamel · cover the occlusal surface of ¾ crowns on premolars where indicated · protect weak cusps.

Extension for prevention BE 42: carry margins to self-cleansable areas: the gingival sulcus, the axial line angles, the suprabulge areas and the inclined planes of cusps.

Future dental health is covered under six headings BE 47–51: axial reduction, margin placement, margin adaptation, margin geometry, occlusion and fracture prevention.

Thin cut, fat crownUnder-reduced axial walls make an over-contoured crown that traps plaque.
Clean places: SALISulcus, Axial line angles, suprabulge (Lumps above contour), Inclined planes.
The onlay (cusp coverage) prevents fracture better than the inlay. The suprabulge is self-cleansable; the infrabulge is the undercut.

Biological record · slides 52–56

Esthetic considerations

  • A good colour match needs a minimum thickness of ceramic, which only comes from adequate, uniform facial reduction BE 53.
  • Esthetics must never be bought at the cost of oral health.
  • For metal-ceramic crowns, esthetics depends on the facial, incisal and proximal reduction and on where the labial margin is placed BE 54–55.
No room, no beautyWithout enough facial reduction the ceramic is too thin to match the shade.
Esthetic demands do not override the biologic principle.

Ceramic preparation · slides 3–51

All-ceramic crowns: why, when and when not

Demand for ceramic crowns has risen by about 50% every four years CP 4. A ceramic jacket crown gets its strength from the ceramic itself; the older porcelain jacket crown has a weaker core of aluminous or feldspathic porcelain CP 7.

Problems with PFM that all-ceramic avoids CP 11–20

  • Exposed metal rim when the gingiva recedes CP 11.
  • Dark shadow: the metal blocks light CP 13; an all-ceramic crown transmits light CP 14.
  • Corrosion at the marginal periodontium, of the metal surface, and of root dentine when different metals are used for post, core and crown CP 16–18.
  • Localized periodontal inflammation around metal-ceramic crowns CP 20.

Advantages CP 9–19

Superior esthetics · translucency · biocompatibility · good tissue response, even with subgingival margins.

Disadvantages CP 23–26

Reduced strength (brittle, fractures) · wear of opposing teeth · high laboratory cost.

Indications CP 29–36

Large defects · fractured anteriors (≤ 1/3 incisogingivally) · discoloured, malformed or malposed teeth · single crowns · bridge retainers only with In-Ceram · high esthetic demand · favourable load · intact incisal edges.

Contraindications CP 39–51

A more conservative option possible · deep or edge-to-edge bite (half-moon fracture) · short clinical crowns · bruxism · violent sports or hard jobs · young patient with a large pulp · careless young patients · high caries index · low esthetic demand · thin teeth · when superior strength is needed (use PFM).

PFM’s four sins: Rim, Shadow, Rust, Red gumExposed metal rim, dark shadow, corrosion, localized gingival inflammation.
Fractured anteriors are an indication only up to one-third incisogingivally. All-ceramic bridge retainers are allowed only with In-Ceram.

Ceramic preparation · slides 52–125

All-ceramic crown preparation, step by step

Armamentarium CP 54

Needle stone · cylindrical round end · cylindrical round angle · round edge wheel · football · tapered round end.

Reduction amounts CP 55

Incisal 1.5–2.0 mm · facial 1.2–1.4 mm · lingual 1.0–1.2 mm · marginal 1.0–1.2 mm.

Putty index CP 56–59: covers at least one tooth on each side. Sectioned at the incisal edges into incisal and gingival halves, it gives no incisal information; sectioned midsagittally (the distal half is kept), it does show the incisal edge.

StepInstrumentKey points
1 · Incisal CP 61–72Flat-end tapered diamond; finish with round edge wheel or flat end1.5–2 mm clearance; flat 45° incisolingual bevel so forces meet the edge at right angles; 3 depth grooves 1.3–1.8 mm
2 · Facial CP 74–91Flat-end tapered diamondTwo planes. Incisal half: 2 grooves 0.8 mm parallel to the incisal facial surface. Gingival half: 3 grooves 0.8 mm parallel to the path. Roughs in the shoulder
3 · Proximal CP 94–98Needle diamond, then flat-end taperedAbout 1 mm; keep the needle inside the tooth
4 · Lingual CP 103–114Flat-end tapered for the cingulum; football for the fossaCingulum wall parallel to the path; fossa 0.7 mm mark measured with a periodontal probe; keep the curved junction and the canine ridge
5 · Finishing CP 116–121Finishing diamonds, carbide burs, binangle chisel, 1.0 mm enamel hatchetRound line angles, refine and plane the shoulder

Measuring the stone CP 62–66: depth grooves are cut with a diamond of known diameter. The micrometer is most accurate but expensive; the caliper is accurate but the stone is hard to secure in its pointed clamps; the endodontic ruler is least accurate and gives a rough idea only.

Why two facial planes? CP 74–78 One plane parallel to the path leaves too little room for porcelain incisally, so the crown is over-contoured or too thin. Cutting that one plane deeper to make room endangers the pulp and over-tapers the preparation.

Details that get examined: mesiodistally the facial reduction follows the original axial contour CP 79; the lingual shoulder follows the free gingiva whenever possible CP 105; axial surfaces are smoothed with a tapered fissure bur CP 118; large-diameter, extra-long finishing burs are less likely to nick the tooth CP 119; the binangle chisel planes the shoulder and removes loose enamel rods CP 120.

Verification CP 122–124: the horizontal facial index checks facial reduction at mid-preparation; the midsagittal index shows the overall reduction distally. The finished preparation is shown on CP 124.

2, 1.4, 1.2, 1.2Upper limits: incisal 2.0 · facial 1.4 · lingual 1.2 · margin 1.2 mm (ranges 1.5–2.0, 1.2–1.4, 1.0–1.2, 1.0–1.2).
Three, two, threeThree incisal grooves; then two incisal-half and three gingival-half facial grooves.
Football for the FossaThe lingual fossa is shaped with the football diamond after a 0.7 mm mark.
Groove depths differ: incisal 1.3–1.8 mm, facial 0.8 mm, fossa mark 0.7 mm. The facial table says 1.2–1.4 mm (CP 55) while step 2 says “about 1 mm”.

Ceramic preparation · slides 80–83, 126–137

Finish lines, errors and preparation guidelines

Recommended finish lines CP 81

Modified shoulder or deep chamfer. Do not leave a lip on the margin CP 82.

Margin design CP 83

1.0 mm shoulder · at least 1.0 mm lingual clearance · 1.5–2.0 mm incisal · rounded axial-gingival line angle.

Clinical errors CP 127–134

  • Excessive reduction with pulp exposure in the incisal third CP 127, or mesially CP 128; excessive reduction near the root dentine CP 129.
  • Excessive taper with a wrong finish line: a shoulder of more than 120° CP 130.
  • Excessive vestibular and insufficient palatal reduction CP 131.
  • J-margin CP 132: the diamond’s apex passes the edge of the margin and cuts a groove inside it. Result: inaccurate scanning, poor fit and thin, fragile porcelain. Prevent it by choosing a bur so the chamfer depth is no more than half the bur tip width.
  • Gutter preparation with an unsupported, easily fractured enamel lip CP 133, and its correction CP 134.

Common errors: “NO!” CP 135

J-shaped margin · square shoulder · rough margin · irregular grooves.

CAD/CAM “Avoid” CP 135

Parallel sides (no milled cement space) · knife edge (coping failure; thin visible zirconia or an over-built profile) · undercuts and sharp edges (must be blocked out).

All-ceramic preparation guidelines CP 136: 1.5–2.0 mm incisal or occlusal · 1.0–1.5 mm axial · 1.0 mm at the margin · shoulder 1.0–1.5 mm wide · taper 5–15°.

J = Jagged lipA J-margin is a groove inside the margin; keep the chamfer depth at most half the bur tip.
Ceramic preps hate the extremesNot parallel, not knife edge, not square, not undercut.
Taper on the all-ceramic guideline slide is 5–15°; the mechanical lecture’s ideal is 3–5°. A square shoulder is a “NO!”; a modified shoulder is recommended.

Memory aids

Hooks, numbers and traps

Read these out loud, then test yourself in the Flashcards. The key-facts grid is your last-hour sheet.

How questions catch you

Trick 1Which lecture’s taper?

3–5° is the mechanical ideal (MR 69); 5–15° is the CAD/CAM slide (CP 136).

Trick 2Retention or resistance

Along the path of insertion = retention. Apical, oblique, horizontal = resistance.

Trick 3Swapped numbers

Incisal 1.5–2.0 · facial 1.2–1.4 · lingual 1.0–1.2; grooves 1.3–1.8, 0.8, fossa 0.7.

Trick 4Which instrument?

Needle → proximal; football → fossa; flat-end tapered → incisal, facial, cingulum; hatchet → shoulder.

Trick 5Indication or contraindication

Discoloured, malformed, malposed = indications. Bruxism, deep bite, short crown, big pulp = contraindications.

Trick 6Direction words

Mesial and distal diverge; infrabulge is the undercut; smaller diameter resists better.
